newsitem.title: USA: U.S. rights group sues Algerian fundamentalist.
newsitem.headline: U.S. rights group sues Algerian fundamentalist.

text.p: A U.S. constitutional rights group said Wednesday it sued a senior Algerian Moslem fundamentalist politician and his group, demanding compensation for alleged human rights violations.

The New York-based Centre for Constitutional Rights said the lawsuit, filed late Tuesday in federal court in Washington, D.C., named the Islamic Salvation Front (FIS) and its self-styled leader, Anouar Haddam.

It said the suit was brought on behalf of plaintiffs representing more than 1,500 women and men, including journalists, political democrats, intellectuals, non-Algerian citizens and opponents of religious intolerance.
The lawsuit seeks unspecified compensatory and punitive damages "for crimes against humanity, war crimes and other gross human rights and humanitarian law violations." It also seeks a jury trial.
Joining in bringing the lawsuit were the International Women's Rights Law Clinic and a Washington, D.C., law firm.

U.S. immigration officials took Haddam into custody this month after denying him political asylum. Haddam, who entered the United States in 1993, is being held pending a hearing to exclude him from the United States.
He was served with the lawsuit Wednesday.

Haddam was elected to parliament in the first round of an Algerian general election in December 1991 but the army intervened to cancel the runoff in January 1992 and prevent an almost certain FIS victory.
The Islamic party was outlawed and its leaders were locked up or exiled. Haddam and his family then took refuge in the United States.
At least 50,000 people have been killed in ensuing violence between the military-dominated authorities and Moslem guerrillas.
